precepts.text: There went with us also certain of the disciples of Caesarea. I just wanted to show you: you had some disciples that came from Caesarea as well, the same place Cornelius is from.
precepts.point: If y'all wasn't in Bishop Kani's class, it's called Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common, maybe two months ago. He goes really slow on it and it's excellent.

note.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell

precepts.why:
Cornelius was “a certain man in Cesarea”. Write this down: Caesarea is in the land of Israel. It is in the land of West Manasseh, right beside Samaria. It is not some foreign country; it is the land of the northern kingdom.

And Acts shows believers coming out of that very place: “There went with us also certain of the disciples of Cesarea, and brought with them one Mnason of Cyprus, an old disciple, with whom we should lodge.” You had some disciples that came from Caesarea as well, the same place Cornelius is from.

Peter lived in Joppa, the seaport there, and he sailed up north to visit Cornelius. Christ was raised further up, in Galilee, so he was raised around them in that area. And the place called Scythopolis means city of the Scythians, and the Scythians are northern kingdom also: that is who Paul wrote to in Colossians 3:11.

So Caesarea was a place of disciples in the land of Manasseh, and Cornelius and his kinsmen were northern kingdom Israelites living in their own land, not a Roman people God took in instead of Israel.

precepts.text: Paul taught all the Jews which are among the Gentiles. We know from the text that the Jews were going to be dispersed among the Gentiles and live like Gentiles. The New Testament shows Paul going out to find the Jews scattered among the other nations, living like strangers and heathens, and bringing them back to God. The job was to raise up the twelve tribes of Israel again.
precepts.point: The majority of the masses did not have what we call the Old Testament. It was the learned men that had the parchments, and it was their job to instruct the people. But now God gave it to the apostles to teach.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
The New Testament shows the dispersed being taught: “And they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to walk after the customs.” There were Jews among the Gentiles, and Paul was going to them.

We know from the text that the Jews were going to be dispersed among the Gentiles and live like Gentiles. Coming back to the New Testament, it shows Paul going out to find the Jews scattered among these other nations, living like Gentiles, living like strangers, living like heathens, and bringing them back to God.

This was the prophecy sent from the Old Testament: the job was to raise up the twelve tribes of Israel again. What the Jews in John 7 asked, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles”?, is exactly what was done.

precepts.text: Judah mourneth; they are black unto the ground.
precepts.point: The chief captain asked Paul, art not thou that Egyptian? Joseph, Moses and Paul all passed for Egyptians.

note.label: False New Year: Doctrine Slayer - True Past Curses & Trauma

precepts.why:
When Paul was led into the castle, the chief captain asked, “Canst thou speak Greek? Art not thou that Egyptian, which before these days madest an uproar, and leddest out into the wilderness four thousand men that were murderers?” He took Paul for a specific Egyptian. “But Paul said, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus”. Paul passed for an Egyptian. Moses passed for an Egyptian. Joseph passed for an Egyptian. Christ passed too: his family ran into Africa from white folks. What more do you possibly need at this point?

Jeremiah shows what Judah looked like: “Judah mourneth, and the gates thereof languish; they are black unto the ground; and the cry of Jerusalem is gone up.” Jeremiah is speaking of the same situation he wrote of in Lamentations, when Babylon came, overthrew us and starved us. We became blacker to the ground: dark, swelled bellies, ribs showing, ribs touching. That is how we looked when Babylon besieged us for those years.

Some try to say it is only symbolic. No: it is the same thing, and Jeremiah, who wrote Lamentations, is saying the same thing in both places. Calling it symbolic is simple and unfaithful and weak.

So the chief captain looking at a Jew and seeing an Egyptian makes sense. Judah was black, and a Jew of Tarsus could pass for an Egyptian because our people looked like the people of Africa. Israel sits in Western Asia bordering North Africa, one land mass, and all the native inhabitants of that region were nonwhite.

precepts.text: The chief captain took Paul for that Egyptian which made an uproar; Paul answered, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus; the Israelites were mistaken for Egyptians.
precepts.point: Reuel the priest of Midian is the same man called Jethro, the father in law of Moses.
precepts.why:
The daughters told their father, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds”. They took Moses for an Egyptian by his dress, by how he carried himself, and by his skin: Moses was a very dark-skinned man, the same color as the Egyptians.

Israel was always being mistaken for Egyptians. When Paul was to be led into the castle, the chief captain asked him, “Canst thou speak Greek? Art not thou that Egyptian, which before these days madest an uproar, and leddest out into the wilderness four thousand men that were murderers?” Paul had to tell him, “I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city”. An Israelite, taken for an Egyptian, from Moses to Paul.

And Moses, who stood up against the shepherds and watered the flock, was a man of war, not a weak man.

precepts.text: The chief captain took Paul for that Egyptian; Israel resembled the Egyptians in appearance.
precepts.point: The difference was made plain in the plague itself: the houses whose firstborn died were shown not to be his people.

note.label: Exodus 11: The Death of the Firstborn Announced

precepts.why:
Long after Egypt, the resemblance was still there. When Paul was taken in Jerusalem, the chief captain asked him, “Art not thou that Egyptian, which before these days madest an uproar, and leddest out into the wilderness four thousand men that were murderers?” Paul, an Israelite, was taken for that Egyptian. Israel resembled the Egyptians in appearance.

That is why the Lord had to put a difference between them in Egypt. If Moses could be taken for an Egyptian, and Paul could be taken for an Egyptian, then the difference the Lord made was not one anyone could see in a face. It was shown by his hand, when not a dog moved his tongue against Israel and the firstborn of Egypt died.

precepts.text: Thousands of Jews which believe, all zealous of the law, and Jews among the Gentiles; Paul purified himself with the four men that had a vow, walking orderly and keeping the law.
precepts.point: The elders at Jerusalem told Paul to purify himself with four men which had a vow on them and be at charges with them, that all may know thou thyself walkest orderly and keepest the law. And note it well: the thousands there that believed were Jews, all zealous of the law, and the Gentiles Paul taught among were Jews scattered among the Gentiles.

note.label: Numbers 6: The Law of the Nazarite and the Blessing of Israel

precepts.why:
The elders at Jerusalem told Paul: “Thou seest, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are which believe; and they are all zealous of the law: And they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to walk after the customs.”

Note it well: the thousands there that believed were Jews, all zealous of the law, and the Gentiles Paul taught among were Jews scattered among the Gentiles.

“Do therefore this that we say to thee: We have four men which have a vow on them; Them take, and purify thyself with them, and be at charges with them, that they may shave their heads: and all may know that those things, whereof they were informed concerning thee, are nothing; but that thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law.” The shaving of the head and the charges of the offering are the Nazarite purification of Numbers 6. Paul purified himself with the four men that had a vow, walking orderly and keeping the law.

precepts.text: How many thousands of Jews there are which believe, and are all zealous of the law, proving belief was coupled with keeping the law.
precepts.point: This five thousand disproves the Christian claim that the Jews all rejected Christ. He came unto his own, meaning the religious leaders, the builders, the chief priests and rulers whose job was to guide the nation, and only those upper echelons rejected him, while thousands of the people believed and were zealous of the law.

note.label: Acts 4: The Stone the Builders Rejected

precepts.why:
Years later the brethren told Paul, “Thou seest, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are which believe; and they are all zealous of the law”.

Many thousands of Jews believed, and their belief was coupled with keeping the law. The five thousand of Acts 4 kept growing, and it was never a people who rejected Christ; it was a people who believed and were zealous of the law.
